descripcion_es: always, usually, often…; -ly adverbs and their position in the sentence.
resumen: Adverbs of frequency (always, often, never…) say how often something happens. They go before the main verb but after be. Adverbs of manner (quickly, well…) say how something is done. They usually go after the verb and its object.

filas: some of the time (es: a veces)
not often, almost never (es: rara vez)

items: Before the main verb: I usually get up at seven.
After be: She is always late.
Between the auxiliary and the main verb: I have never seen it. / You can always call me.
Sometimes and usually can also go at the start: Sometimes we eat out.
Expressions like every day, once a week, twice a month go at the end: I go swimming twice a week.

explicacion.texto: Adverbs of manner are almost always formed with adjective + -ly: slow → slowly, careful → carefully, easy → easily, gentle → gently. Irregular: good → well; fast, hard, late and early do not change. Hardly means “almost not” (es: apenas) and lately means “recently” (es: últimamente): they are not the adverbs of hard and late.
The adverb of manner does not go between the verb and its direct object: She speaks English fluently, not She speaks fluently English.

Adjective or adverb: the adjective describes a noun (He's a careful driver) and the adverb describes the verb (He drives carefully). After look, feel, seem, sound or taste you use an adjective: You look tired.

ejemplos.frase: We often have lunch in the garden.
ejemplos.traduccion: A menudo comemos en el jardín.

ejemplos.frase: He is never at home on Sundays.
ejemplos.traduccion: Nunca está en casa los domingos.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I go always to work by bus.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I always go to work by bus.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The adverb of frequency goes before the main verb.
With be, the adverb goes after it.
To describe how something is done you need the -ly adverb, not the adjective.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I play very well the guitar.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I play the guitar very well.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The adverb of manner does not separate the verb from its object.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the adverb of manner of the adjective in brackets.
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the rule on the card for forming adverbs of manner: adjective + -ly. The clue is that the word describes how the action “listen” is done, so you need an adverb, not the adjective “careful”. Just add -ly to “careful”: careful + ly = carefully, with a double l because the adjective already ends in -l. You don't remove any letters.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Careful” is the adjective; to describe how someone listens you need the adverb “carefully”.
An l is missing: the adjective already ends in -l and you add the whole of -ly, so there are two: carefully.
This word does not exist: the suffix is -ful with one l, and the adverb also needs -ly.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the adverb of manner of the adjective in brackets.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the most important irregular adverb on the card: the adverb of “good” is “well”, not “goodly”. The clue is that the word describes how Grandma cooks, so it modifies the verb “cooks”: you need an adverb. “Very well” is the Spanish “muy bien”. “Good” could only go with a noun (“a good cook”) or after verbs like look or feel.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The adverb of good is well.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Good” is an adjective; to describe how someone cooks you use the adverb “well”. In informal American speech you hear “cooks good”, but the standard is “well”.
“Goodly” is not the adverb of “good”: it is an old word that means “considerable”. The adverb is “well”.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the adverb of manner of the adjective in brackets.
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the card's spelling rule for adverbs of manner: when the adjective ends in consonant + y, the y changes to i before -ly. The clue is that the word says how she passed, so it needs the adverb. That is why easy → easily, like happy → happily. If you kept the y, the word would be misspelt.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the adjective; you need the adverb. Only in fixed informal expressions like “take it easy” is “easy” used as an adverb.
After a consonant, y changes to i before -ly: easily.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the adverb of manner of the adjective in brackets.
ejercicios.frase: The athletes trained ___ (hard) for the Olympics.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is one of the irregular ones on the card: “hard” has the same form as an adjective and as an adverb. The clue is that the word describes how they trained (with a lot of effort), so it works as an adverb of manner, and its form is still “hard”. The trap is “hardly”, which exists but means “almost not”: “they hardly trained” would mean they almost didn't train, just the opposite.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Hard does not change as an adverb; hardly means “almost not”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los atletas entrenaron duro para los Juegos Olímpicos.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Hardly” means “almost not”; the sentence would say they almost didn't train. The adverb for effort is “hard”.
“Hardy” is a different adjective (strong, tough), not an adverb.

ejercicios.explicacion: Use the card's position rule: the adverb of frequency goes before the main verb. The clue is that “has” here is a main verb (have breakfast) and not an auxiliary, because it is not followed by a past participle. That is why it is “She never has breakfast”, with the adverb in front and the verb in the present simple with -s. If “has” were an auxiliary, the adverb would go after it, but that is not the case here.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The adverb of frequency goes before the main verb.

por_opcion.never has: Correct: adverb of frequency before the main verb “has” (in “have breakfast”).
por_opcion.has never: Incorrect here: the order auxiliary + adverb only works when “has” is the auxiliary of the present perfect (“She has never had breakfast here”); in “has breakfast”, “has” is the main verb.
por_opcion.never is having: Incorrect: the continuous does not express a habit, and the adverb would go after “is” anyway; the natural form for a habit is the present simple.

ejercicios.frase: My boss ___ in a good mood on Mondays.
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the exception the card highlights: with the verb be, the adverb of frequency goes after it, not before. The clue is “in a good mood”, which needs the verb “be”. That is why it is “is rarely”. “Rarely” means “not often”, almost never, and has a negative meaning, so you don't add “not”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With be, the adverb goes after it.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi jefe rara vez está de buen humor los lunes.

por_opcion.is rarely: Correct: with be, the adverb of frequency goes after the verb.
por_opcion.rarely is: Incorrect: that order works with main verbs, but not with be. It is only used in short emphatic answers like “He rarely is”, which is not the case here.
por_opcion.rarely: Incorrect: the verb is missing; “in a good mood” needs “be”.

ejercicios.explicacion: Use the card's rule on adjective or adverb: after look, feel, seem, sound or taste you use an adjective, not an adverb. The clue is the verb “tastes”, which here does not describe an action but a quality of the soup: what its flavour is like. That is why it is “tastes wonderful”, like “looks tired”. Although Spanish says “sabe estupendamente”, in English the -ly adverb would be a mistake.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After taste you use an adjective.

por_opcion.wonderfully: Incorrect: after “taste”, as after look or feel, you use an adjective because it describes the soup, not the way an action is done.
por_opcion.wonderful: Correct: an adjective after the verb of perception “taste”.
por_opcion.wonder: Incorrect: “wonder” is a noun (a marvel) or a verb (to ask yourself); it does not describe the flavour.

ejercicios.explicacion: Use the card's distinction between adjective and adverb: the adjective describes a noun and the adverb describes a verb. The clue is that after the gap comes the noun “driver”, with “a” in front: you need an adjective. That is why it is “a dangerous driver”. With the verb you would use the adverb: “Juan drives dangerously”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: It describes the noun driver: adjective.

por_opcion.dangerous: Correct: an adjective describing the noun “driver”.
por_opcion.dangerously: Incorrect: the adverb describes verbs (“he drives dangerously”), not nouns.
por_opcion.danger: Incorrect: “danger” is the noun; “a danger driver” is not English.

ejercicios.frase: I eat usually at two o'clock.
respuestas: I usually eat at two o'clock.
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the main position rule: the adverb of frequency goes before the main verb. The clue is that “eat” is a main verb and there is no auxiliary or be. The correct sentence is “I usually eat at two o'clock”. The mistake is copying the Spanish “como normalmente”, which puts the adverb after the verb.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Usually goes before the main verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I eat usually at two o'clock.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the adverb cannot go between the verb and its object.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I eat at two o'clock usually.
errores_previstos.explicacion: At the end of the sentence it is understandable, but it is not the normal position of “usually”: it goes before the main verb.

ejercicios.explicacion: Use the card's rule that the adverb of manner does not go between the verb and its direct object. The clue is “Italian”, the direct object of “speak”: it must stay next to the verb. That is why it is “They speak Italian fluently”, with the adverb at the end. Spanish allows “hablan perfectamente italiano”, but English does not separate the verb and the object.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The adverb of manner goes after the object.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the adverb separates the verb from its direct object.
“Fluent” is an adjective (“fluent Italian”); to describe how they speak you need the adverb “fluently”.

ejercicios.explicacion: Use the exception for be: the adverb of frequency goes after this verb. The clue is “are right”, which in English is formed with be (Spanish says “tener razón”). That is why it is “You are often right” or, contracted, “You're often right”. With other verbs it would go before (“You often know the answer”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With be, the adverb goes after it.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: with be, the adverb goes after it, not before.
At the end it sounds unnatural; the normal position of “often” with be is right after the verb.

ejercicios.enunciado: Add the adverb in brackets in the correct position.
respuestas: We have never been to Asia.
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the card's rule for compound tenses: the adverb goes between the auxiliary and the main verb. The clue is “have been”, a present perfect with the auxiliary “have” and the past participle “been”. That is why it is “We have never been to Asia”. “Never” is already negative, so you don't add “not”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Between the auxiliary and the past participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We never have been to Asia.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With an auxiliary, the adverb goes after it and before the past participle: “have never been”. The order “never have” is only used for special emphasis.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We have been never to Asia.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The adverb cannot go after the past participle: it goes between the auxiliary and the participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We haven't never been to Asia.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In standard English there is no double negative: “never” already makes the sentence negative.

respuestas: I always brush my teeth before bed
Before bed I always brush my teeth
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the basic structure on the card: subject + adverb of frequency + main verb + object. The clue is that “brush” is the main verb and there is no auxiliary or be, so “always” goes just before it. Then come the object (“my teeth”) and the time expression (“before bed”), which can also go at the start. That is why both answers are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Subject + adverb of frequency + verb + object.
ejercicios.traduccion: Siempre me lavo los dientes antes de acostarme.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I brush always my teeth before bed
errores_previstos.explicacion: This order is copied from the Spanish “me lavo siempre”: the adverb does not go after the main verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Always I brush my teeth before bed
errores_previstos.explicacion: “Always” does not go at the start of the sentence (only sometimes and usually go there naturally).

ejercicios.explicacion: Use the position rule for adverbs of manner: they usually go after the verb and its object, without separating them. The clue is “closed the door”: “the door” is the direct object and the adverb cannot separate it from the verb. That is why it is “She closed the door quietly”. The position before the verb is also accepted, “She quietly closed the door”, which the card allows and which sounds a little more like a story.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The adverb of manner usually goes after the object; it can also go before the verb.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cerró la puerta sin hacer ruido.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The adverb of manner cannot go between the verb and its direct object.
This order is impossible in English: the subject goes before the verb and the object after it.

respuestas: We go to the gym twice a week
Twice a week we go to the gym
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the card's rule for frequency expressions of several words (every day, once a week, twice a week): they go at the end of the sentence, not before the verb like one-word adverbs. The clue is “twice a week”. The basic sentence is “We go to the gym” and the expression is added after it; it can also go at the start for emphasis. What you cannot do is put it between the subject and the verb.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Expressions like twice a week go at the end.
ejercicios.traduccion: Vamos al gimnasio dos veces por semana.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We twice a week go to the gym
errores_previstos.explicacion: Expressions of several words do not take the position of single-word adverbs before the verb: they go at the end or at the start.

descripcion_larga_es: Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, never) say how often something happens, and adverbs of manner (quickly, carefully, well) say how it is done. The hard part is not the meaning but the position: English word order is much stricter than Spanish, and sentences like “I go always” or “speak fluently English” immediately give away a Spanish speaker.

contexto.que_es: There are two groups of adverbs. Adverbs of frequency say how many times something happens (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never). Adverbs of manner say how the action is done, and almost all of them are formed with adjective + -ly (slow → slowly), with some irregular ones like good → well or hard → hard.
contexto.por_que_importa: They are used all the time to talk about routines, habits and ways of doing things, from the most basic level. Putting them in the wrong place does not usually stop people understanding you, but it sounds very foreign, and in an exam it is a basic mistake that costs a lot. Mixing up adjective and adverb (drive careful, look tiredly) is also a very visible mistake.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: When you describe your routine, talk about habits or explain how someone does something. The signals are questions like “How often…?” (frequency) or “How does he…?” (manner). Spanish speakers put the adverb where it would go in Spanish, after the verb (“voy siempre”, “habla perfectamente inglés”); in English it goes before the main verb or after be, and the adverb of manner goes after the object.
